# Starter log: Doughlores

A running log for the sourdough starter I've named Doughlores, kept going since a jar of flour and
water first started bubbling on the counter. This note is deliberately long and rambling — it's the
one place I dump everything about feeding, troubleshooting, and the recipes that came out of it, so
future me has a single reference instead of six scattered scraps of paper.

## Origins

Doughlores began as a 1:1:1 flour-water-starter culture in a repurposed pickle jar, fed with a mix
of whole wheat and unbleached bread flour for the first two weeks to get a strong yeast and bacteria
population established before switching to an all-purpose maintenance feed. The first week showed
almost no activity beyond a faint sour smell; by day nine it was reliably doubling within six hours
of a feed, which is usually the signal that a wild culture has stabilized.

### Why whole wheat first

Whole wheat flour carries more of the wild yeast and bacteria naturally present on the grain than
heavily milled white flour, so a new culture gets going faster on it. Once the population is
established, switching to all-purpose flour keeps the starter's flavor milder and its behavior more
predictable, since whole wheat continues to ferment noticeably faster even after the culture matures.

### Naming it

Somewhat embarrassing in hindsight, but the name stuck after a friend joked the jar looked like it
belonged in a telenovela. It's on the label now, so it's permanent.

## Feeding schedule

Currently on a twice-daily feed at 100% hydration (equal weight flour and water) when kept at room
temperature, dropping to once a day when the kitchen is warmer than about 24°C, since fermentation
speeds up a lot with ambient heat. When traveling or otherwise not baking for a stretch, Doughlores
goes into the fridge on a reduced feed — once a week is enough to keep it alive, though it comes back
sluggish and needs two or three feeds at room temperature to wake back up properly.

### The discard problem

Discard used to just get thrown away, which felt wasteful given how much flour goes into keeping a
starter alive. Now it goes into crackers, pancakes, or a quick discard flatbread on the griddle —
none of it needs the starter to be active, since the point is using up excess rather than leavening
anything.

### Ratio experiments

Tried a 1:5:5 feed (small amount of starter, large amount of fresh flour and water) to stretch out
the time between feeds for a longer trip, and it worked reasonably well — the larger buffer of fresh
food meant it took nearly 24 hours to get hungry again instead of the usual 8 to 12. Worth remembering
next time there's a week away from home without wanting to burden a neighbor with starter-sitting.

## Troubleshooting

### The hooch incident

A layer of dark liquid appeared on top of the starter after a stretch of neglect — this is hooch, a
sign the culture is hungry and has run out of food to ferment, not a sign anything has gone wrong or
spoiled. Poured most of it off, stirred the rest back in, and did two back-to-back feeds twelve hours
apart to bring the culture back to a normal rhythm. It bounced back within a day.

### A worrying smell

At one point the starter developed a smell closer to acetone or nail polish remover than the usual
pleasant sour tang. This is apparently common and just means the culture is very hungry and producing
a lot of alcohol as a byproduct — again, not spoilage, just an aggressive feeding schedule needed. A
couple of feeds with a bit less flour and more frequent timing sorted it out within two days.

### Pink or orange spots

Never actually happened to Doughlores, but it's worth writing down here because it's the one true
red flag: pink, orange, or fuzzy spots mean an actual unwanted mold or bacteria has taken hold, and
the whole jar needs to be thrown out and restarted from scratch rather than fed through. Everything
else — hooch, odd smells, sluggish rises — is normal starter behavior, not spoilage.

## Recipes that came out of this starter

### The Tuesday loaf

A basic 75% hydration country loaf, mixed the night before, bulk fermented on the counter for about
five hours with a few sets of stretch-and-folds in the first two hours, shaped, and left in the
fridge overnight for a cold retard before baking straight from cold in a preheated Dutch oven. This
is the everyday loaf — nothing fancy, but it's reliable enough that this recipe alone justified
keeping the starter going through a busy month when nothing else got baked.

### Discard crackers

Mixed roughly equal parts discard and flour with a pinch of salt and a glug of olive oil, rolled
thin, docked with a fork, and baked until crisp. Rosemary or everything-bagel seasoning both work
well pressed into the top before baking. This is the default answer to "what do I do with all this
discard" and gets made more often than the bread itself some weeks.

### The higher-hydration attempt

Pushed a batch to 85% hydration to chase a more open, irregular crumb, which meant handling the
dough almost entirely with wet hands and a bowl scraper rather than a floured board. The result was
noticeably more open than the Tuesday loaf but also much harder to shape, and the loaf spread flatter
than intended during the final proof. Worth revisiting with a stronger banneton and a colder final
proof next time, but not going into regular rotation as-is.

## Equipment notes

The Dutch oven that gets used for every bake is a plain enameled cast iron pot, preheated with the
oven for 45 minutes before the dough goes in — the stored heat in the pot walls is what gives the
oven-spring and the crust color, more than the oven's own ambient temperature. A cheap infrared
thermometer pointed at the pot's interior confirmed it actually reaches the oven's set temperature
by the end of preheating, which a quick hand-test near the door never would have told me.

### Lame and scoring

Switched from a paring knife to a proper lame for scoring, and the ears on the finished loaves
improved immediately — a fresh double-edge blade held at a shallow angle gives a clean, decisive cut
that opens up during oven-spring instead of tearing raggedly. Worth keeping a small stash of spare
blades on hand, since a dull one drags through the crust instead of slicing it and undoes most of
the benefit of switching away from the knife in the first place.

## Flour notes

### Local mill versus supermarket bag

Switched to a bag of flour from a small local mill for a stretch, mostly out of curiosity, and the
loaves came out with a noticeably nuttier flavor and a slightly darker crumb than the usual
supermarket bread flour. Hydration needed a small downward adjustment too — the local mill's flour
drank less water before the dough felt right, which tracks with it being milled a little coarser.
Worth keeping a bag around for special-occasion bakes even though the everyday flour stays the cheap
supermarket one, mostly for cost and consistency reasons rather than any complaint about quality.

### Storage

Flour lives in a sealed bin on the counter rather than the bag it ships in, both to keep pantry moths
out and to stop it from drying out or picking up smells from anything else stored nearby. Whole wheat
goes in the fridge instead, since the bran's oils go rancid noticeably faster at room temperature than
the more refined bread flour does, and a rancid batch has ruined more than one loaf's flavor before
the cause was finally tracked down to the flour itself rather than anything in the process.

## Lessons learned

The single biggest improvement to consistency wasn't a technique change at all — it was switching to
weighing everything on a kitchen scale instead of using volume measurements for flour and water.
Flour especially varies a lot by how it's scooped, and that variance was quietly wrecking hydration
percentages before the switch. Second biggest lesson: writing down what actually happened, including
the failures, instead of only the recipe that worked, is the only reason any of the troubleshooting
notes above exist to reference the next time something looks wrong.
